source.title: WISE: Weak-Supervision-Guided Step-by-Step Explanations for Multimodal LLMs in Image Classification
source.authors: Yi-Wen Jiang; Deval Mehta; Si-Yuan Yan; Ya-Ling Shen; Zimu Wang; Zong-Yuan Ge

page_placements.theme: Properties other than accuracy under W2S: fairness, privacy, calibration, inherited data bias, interpretability

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: Applies weak-supervision-guided fine-tuning to multimodal image classification and reports classification outcomes, extending the idea to a vision setting. It does not measure PGR or make a matched comparison showing the student outperforming its weak supervisor.
record.gate_note: The paper uses weak-supervisor-generated concept annotations and rationales to fine-tune an MLLM, but compares its accuracy mainly with instruction tuning without rationales, not with the weak supervisor under a matched evaluation setup. Weak-supervisor and MLLM evaluation setups differ: the paper states that MLLMs use open-set classification while weak supervisors use closed-set classification. No PGR is reported. The paper also reports interpretability results, which are not the classification effect named in V6.
record.test_reason: The paper borrows the weak-to-strong idea as motivation and as a tool. CLIP, CBM, decision-tree and Naive Bayes supervisors generate concept rationales (MCoTs). Qwen2-VL-7B is then fine-tuned on these rationales together with the gold category labels. The student never trains on weak class labels. Its accuracy is compared only with instruction tuning without rationales (IT-IO), which compares two variants of the authors' method under gold supervision. Accuracy against the weak supervisors is not matched: the authors say the MLLM uses open-set classification and the supervisors closed-set. For the concept-annotated datasets, concept labels come from ground-truth annotations filtered for CLIP salience, not from weak predictions. The one student-beats-supervisor result is on interpretability, scored with metrics defined differently per supervisor. That is a related construct, so it is recorded under fits_no_version. No version, including V6, is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors' headline is interpretability: MCoTs from weak supervision improve MLLM interpretability by 37% over zero-shot MCoT, and on average exceed the best weak supervisor. Accuracy rises by 0.69% on average over IT-IO, with minor drops on two datasets and comparable results on Oxford-Pets and Oxford-Flowers.
record.recipe_differences: Rather than fine-tuning directly on weak-model task labels and measuring PGR, WISE uses CLIP/CBM-derived concept annotations and decision-tree-generated rationales, then fine-tunes an MLLM. Its principal accuracy comparison is instruction tuning without rationales. The paper does not report a matched student-versus-supervisor accuracy comparison.
record.method_sensitivity: Accuracy changes across datasets: unchanged on SkinCon-3, decreases on LAD-F and LAD-V, and varies on the other reported datasets. Oxford-Pets decreases while Oxford-Flowers increases slightly.

fits_no_version.finding: The fine-tuned MLLM's average interpretability (concept precision) is 87.83%. This exceeds the best weak supervisor, the decision tree at 79.64%. The MLLM falls short of its supervisor on only two of eight datasets (Table 1). The supervisors' interpretability metrics are each defined differently.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A strong multimodal model fine-tuned on rationales built from weak supervisors can exceed those supervisors' concept-level explanation precision.

record.peer_reviewed: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP), as stated in the supplied study metadata; the provided paper text identifies itself as an arXiv preprint.
record.problems: The paper does not report PGR or a matched comparison against the weak supervisor. It explicitly uses different evaluation setups for weak supervisors and MLLMs (closed-set versus open-set classification). No uncertainty estimates are given for the reported accuracy results.
record.rows_left_out: Weak-supervisor accuracy and MLLM interpretability results are not included as rows: they do not provide the matched student-versus-supervisor outcome or classification effect named by V6. No results were omitted from the relevant MLLM accuracy comparisons.

untested.parts: No matched comparison of the student against the weak supervisor, and no PGR. The student is trained on gold class labels.
No variation of supervisor or student size, and no PGR analysis.
No tests of exploitation, distribution shift or shared errors.
No theory of when a student must beat its supervisor.
No weak-label-only training in vision. There is no matched accuracy comparison between student and supervisor (open-set vs closed-set), and no PGR.

record.verdict_notes: No verdicts are given because no version is tested. The record's V6 supports and limits_scope labels rest on IT-MCoT vs IT-IO comparisons. In those comparisons both arms use gold labels, so they measure the effect of adding rationales, not weak-to-strong generalization. Raw weak-supervisor accuracies in Table 1 are mostly below the MLLM's. The authors say these setups are not comparable, and the MLLM had gold labels anyway.

versions.untested_parts: No matched test of whether the strong student beats the weak supervisor or recovers a performance gap.
No tested auxiliary confidence loss, ensembling of weak supervisors, or loss variant raising PGR.
No PGR analysis across supervisor or student sizes, tasks, or representations.
No tests of exploitability, distribution shift, or shared student-supervisor errors.
No theoretical conditions for a student beating its supervisor.
Tests weak-supervision-guided MLLM fine-tuning for image classification, but not a matched student-versus-supervisor comparison or PGR.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

relation.reason: The weak-to-strong principle motivates rationale supervision; training retains dataset category labels. The supervisor comparison measures concept precision rather than the catalog's weak-label generalization effect.

tranche.reason: WISE uses weak supervision to construct rationales and reports its method's classification accuracy and concept precision. It does not test recovery of task performance from weak class labels.

source_check.notes: Table 1 and Section 4.3 confirm 87.83% average concept precision versus 79.64% for decision trees. The student falls below decision-tree precision on CUB and LAD-A.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: CUB, SkinCon-9, LAD-A, LAD-E, LAD-H, Oxford-Flowers, and the reported eight-dataset average
reader_labels.reason: WISE MCoT fine-tuning improves accuracy over instruction tuning without rationales in these settings, though the gains are small or incomplete; see r1, r3–r6, r9, and r11.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: Accuracy is unchanged or lower than the no-MCoT instruction-tuning baseline in these settings; see r2, r7, r8, and r10.
